READING

**Building the numbers season by season**

Start with what the 640 colonies earn doing nothing but honey: £143,000 a year, £223.44 a colony. Of that, borage contributes £71 a colony; heather therefore contributes £152.44 a colony (£143,000 − 640 × £71 = £97,560 heather; £97,560 ÷ 640 = £152.44).

Under TREVANNOCK the 400 orchard colonies still do heather but miss borage. Annual honey income becomes:

- Heather across all 640: £97,560
- Borage on the 240 colonies that stay home: 240 × £71 = £17,040
- Honey total: £114,600

Add the Vantwyn fee: 400 × £168 = £67,200.

Subtract spray losses: 9% of 400 = 36 colonies × £210 = £7,560.

Subtract haulage: £6,900.

**TREVANNOCK annual net income: £114,600 + £67,200 − £7,560 − £6,900 = £167,340**

**ORMSCLEUCH annual net income: £143,000** (all 640 on own sites, no haulage, no spray mortality).

Annual advantage to TREVANNOCK: **£24,340**.

Over three seasons that is £73,020.

Now the kit. Ravensgate pays £96,000 now. Under TREVANNOCK the lorry becomes a farm vehicle at roughly £20,000 the moment the vale low-emission permit lapses on 2030-01-01; the pallets have some residual value but no figure is offered and they will have had three further working seasons of wear. Call the total terminal value of the kit conservatively at £20,000.

Kit opportunity cost: £96,000 − £20,000 = **£76,000 in favour of ORMSCLEUCH**.

Three-season scoreboard, undiscounted:

| | ORMSCLEUCH | TREVANNOCK |
|---|---|---|
| Kit proceeds | +£96,000 | +£20,000 (residual, end 2029) |
| Three-season net income | +£429,000 | +£502,020 |
| **Total** | **£525,000** | **£522,020** |

The gap is about £3,000 in ORMSCLEUCH's favour before any time-value adjustment. Receiving £96,000 in August 2026 is meaningfully better than receiving £20,000 in late 2029; even at a modest 5 % discount rate the present value of that £20,000 is roughly £17,000, widening the gap to nearer £8,000. The numbers are not a landslide, but the direction is clear and consistent.

**Stress-testing the TREVANNOCK case**

*Spray losses.* The 9 % figure comes from one operator on one comparable programme. It is not a guarantee; it is a floor-level data point from a single season. If losses run to 12 % (48 colonies, £10,080) instead of 9 %, the annual advantage of TREVANNOCK falls from £24,340 to £21,820, and the cumulative three-year advantage falls to £65,460 — still well short of the kit differential. Surviving colonies that have been through pesticide stress also tend to be weaker going into the heather flow; that erosion of honey yield is not captured in the replacement-cost figure at all.

*Vantwyn's non-negotiable spray programme.* They will not vary it. That means no recourse if losses exceed what the contract contemplates. Fenella carries all the biological risk.

*The lorry permit.* Even if Fenella wanted to continue in the vale after 2029, the Hiab loses its permit on 2030-01-01. Continued vale operations would require either a new compliant vehicle or hired haulage, neither of which is costed. The kit is not a permanent platform for a pollination business — it has a hard expiry.

*Previous track record.* Three contracts funded the migratory build-out; none has renewed. That is weak evidence that Fenella's operation commands sticky relationships in the pollination market.

**The vale upside**

Coldharbour and Nyefield are asking for rates, not offering signed contracts. Even if both committed to, say, 200 colonies each for 2028, Fenella has only 240 colonies not already committed to Vantwyn, so filling both new contracts would gut the home sites entirely and multiply spray exposure. The upside exists but is constrained by colony count and competes directly with the honey income the orchard placements already compromise.

**Qualitative balance**

TREVANNOCK keeps a door open. ORMSCLEUCH closes it deliberately and permanently. That matters — but the door it closes leads into a market where Fenella's three previous relationships all lapsed, where the key lorry becomes a limited-use farm vehicle in three years regardless, and where the financial case for staying in is essentially a wash even before risk adjustment. Simplicity, colony health, and a clean balance sheet are genuine operational goods, not just consolation prizes.

**Conclusion**

The raw three-year arithmetic lands within £3,000–£8,000 of break-even and ORMSCLEUCH is on the right side of it. Once spray-loss risk, time value of the up-front payment, and the 2030 lorry-permit cliff are layered in, ORMSCLEUCH is the stronger course. The Ravensgate offer closes 2026-11-28, well inside the Vantwyn decision window of 2026-10-31, so declining Vantwyn and accepting Ravensgate can be executed in a clean sequence this autumn.

---

READING
  The three-year operating advantage of TREVANNOCK (£73,020) is almost exactly cancelled by the kit-sale opportunity cost (£76,000). In that near-tie, ORMSCLEUCH holds the additional margins of £96,000 received now rather than a degraded residual in 2029, no spray-mortality exposure on a programme Vantwyn will not vary, freedom from the 2030 lorry-permit cliff, and a simpler single-business operation — while the vale upside under TREVANNOCK is genuine but constrained by colony count and is unsupported by any committed contract from Coldharbour or Nyefield.

CALL
  ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
  The three-year income advantage of taking the Vantwyn contract is almost exactly offset by the foregone Ravensgate proceeds, so the decisive margin belongs to ORMSCLEUCH: £96,000 received with certainty in autumn 2026, no spray-loss liability on a programme Vantwyn will not adjust, and no lorry-permit cliff in 2030 — together they tip a near-tied financial case firmly toward the simpler course.
